kcet|Chemistry|2013|27||0|0.s:
Acetophenone is C₆H₅COCH₃ — a benzene ring carrying an **acyl** group, CH₃CO–.
Putting an acyl group onto a ring is Friedel–Crafts acylation, using an acid chloride or anhydride
with anhydrous AlCl₃:
C₆H₆ + CH₃COCl --AlCl₃--> C₆H₅COCH₃ + HCl
The AlCl₃ generates the electrophile, the acylium ion CH₃CO⁺, which the ring attacks.
Friedel–Crafts **alkylation** (3) would attach CH₃– and give toluene, not a ketone — no carbonyl
is introduced.
Wurtz (1) couples two alkyl halides and does not involve an aromatic ring at all, and
Wurtz–Fittig (2) joins an aryl halide to an alkyl halide, giving an alkylbenzene again rather
than a ketone.
Acylation also has the advantage of not rearranging and not polysubstituting, because the
product ketone is deactivated.
∴ Friedel–Crafts acylation.

kcet|Chemistry|2013|28||0|0.s:
PCl₅ replaces an –OH by –Cl, and sulphuric acid has two of them, so the amount of PCl₅ decides
how far the substitution goes.
With one equivalent only the first OH is replaced:
H₂SO₄ + PCl₅ ⇒ HSO₃Cl + POCl₃ + HCl
giving chlorosulphuric acid, option (1).
With **excess** PCl₅ the second OH goes too:
HSO₃Cl + PCl₅ ⇒ SO₂Cl₂ + POCl₃ + HCl
The product is sulphuryl chloride, SO₂Cl₂, in which sulphur keeps its two oxygens and now
carries two chlorines.
Note the word 'excess' in the question is the whole clue; without it the answer would be
chlorosulphuric acid.
Do not confuse SO₂Cl₂ (sulphuryl chloride, S at +6) with SOCl₂ (thionyl chloride, S at +4).
∴ sulphuryl chloride.

kcet|Chemistry|2013|29||0|0:
A neutral buffer has a pH close to 7, and that happens when the salt is formed from a weak
acid and a weak base of **comparable** strength.
Acetic acid (Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵) with ammonium hydroxide (Kb = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵) gives ammonium
acetate. Because Ka and Kb are equal, the hydrolysis of the cation and of the anion cancel
exactly and the solution is neutral:
pH = 7 + ½(pKa − pKb) = 7 + ½(4.74 − 4.74) = 7
(1) NH₄OH with NH₄Cl is a weak base and its salt — a **basic** buffer, pH above 7.
(2) Acetic acid with sodium acetate and (4) citric acid with sodium citrate are weak acids with
their salts — **acidic** buffers, pH below 7.
Only (3) pairs a weak acid with a weak base.
∴ acetic acid and ammonium hydroxide.
kcet|Chemistry|2013|32||0|0:
On the Brønsted–Lowry definition, the conjugate base of an acid is what is left after it has
donated **one** proton.
Start with H₂PO₄⁻ and remove one H⁺:
H₂PO₄⁻ ⇒ H⁺ + HPO₄²⁻
Check the bookkeeping: the hydrogen count falls from 2 to 1, and losing a positive charge makes
the charge go from −1 to −2 ✓
So the conjugate base is HPO₄²⁻.
The other options are a step too far in one direction or the other:
H₃PO₄ is the conjugate **acid** of H₂PO₄⁻, formed by *gaining* a proton.
PO₄³⁻ is two protons away, the conjugate base of HPO₄²⁻, not of H₂PO₄⁻.
HPO₄⁻ as written in option (1) is not even a valid species — the charge does not balance.
Note H₂PO₄⁻ is amphiprotic: it can lose a proton or gain one, which is why it buffers so well.
∴ HPO₄²⁻.

kcet|Chemistry|2013|33||0|0.s:
The Wurtz reaction joins two identical alkyl groups, so the product must be symmetrical and
the new bond lies at its centre.
Draw 4,5-diethyloctane: an eight-carbon chain with an ethyl group on C4 and another on C5.
The molecule is symmetrical about the C4–C5 bond, so that is the bond Wurtz made.
Cut it there and look at one half:
C1–C2–C3–C4, with an ethyl branch on C4
Written out, that fragment is CH₃CH₂CH₂–CH(C₂H₅)–
So the radical had six carbons, with the reactive centre on the third one. Putting the bromine
back where the bond was formed:
X = CH₃CH₂CH₂–CHBr–CH₂CH₃, that is 3-bromohexane.
Check by recombining: two C6 fragments give C12, and 4,5-diethyloctane is C8 + 2(C2) = C12 ✓
∴ CH₃–(CH₂)₂–CH(Br)–CH₂–CH₃.

kcet|Chemistry|2013|34||0|0.s:
Magnetic moment rises with the number of unpaired electrons, μ = √(n(n + 2)) BM.
Write each ion's d configuration, removing the 4s electrons first, and fill by Hund's rule.
Fe²⁺ : Fe is [Ar]3d⁶4s² ⇒ 3d⁶ ⇒ ↑↓ ↑ ↑ ↑ ↑ ⇒ n = 4
Co²⁺ : Co is [Ar]3d⁷4s² ⇒ 3d⁷ ⇒ ↑↓ ↑↓ ↑ ↑ ↑ ⇒ n = 3
Cr³⁺ : Cr is [Ar]3d⁵4s¹ ⇒ 3d³ ⇒ ↑ ↑ ↑ ⇒ n = 3
Ni²⁺ : Ni is [Ar]3d⁸4s² ⇒ 3d⁸ ⇒ ↑↓ ↑↓ ↑↓ ↑ ↑ ⇒ n = 2
The largest n is 4, for Fe²⁺:
μ = √(4 × 6) = √24 = 4.90 BM
against 3.87 for Co²⁺ and Cr³⁺, and 2.83 for Ni²⁺.
∴ Fe²⁺.

kcet|Chemistry|2013|35||0|0:
In a galvanic cell the electrode with the **more negative** reduction potential is oxidised and
becomes the anode.
Zn²⁺|Zn at −0.76 V is more negative than Fe²⁺|Fe at −0.41 V, so zinc is the anode and iron
the cathode.
E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode
= (−0.41) − (−0.76)
= −0.41 + 0.76
= +0.35 V
The positive value confirms the choice: a spontaneous cell must have E°cell > 0, since
ΔG° = −nFE°cell has to be negative.
Had the electrodes been assigned the other way round the answer would have come out −0.35 V,
which is option (1) and the usual error.
The cell reaction is Zn + Fe²⁺ ⇒ Zn²⁺ + Fe.
∴ +0.35 V.

kcet|Chemistry|2013|36||0|0.s:
Check each pairing.
I. RX + aqueous AgOH ⇒ **ROH**, an alcohol, not RH. The hydroxide ion substitutes for the
halide; nothing reduces the carbon. ✗
II. RX + alcoholic AgCN ⇒ RNC ✓ Silver cyanide is largely covalent, so the lone pair that
attacks belongs to the **nitrogen**, giving the isocyanide.
III. RX + alcoholic KCN ⇒ **RCN**, the nitrile, not RNC. KCN is ionic, so the free cyanide ion
attacks through its **carbon**, which is the more nucleophilic end. ✗
IV. RX + Na in dry ether ⇒ R–R ✓ This is the Wurtz reaction, coupling two alkyl groups.
So II and IV are the correctly matched pairs.
II and III together are the classic contrast: the same cyanide group, but AgCN gives the
isocyanide and KCN the nitrile, purely because of ionic against covalent character.
∴ II and IV.

kcet|Chemistry|2013|37||0|0.s:
Paramagnetism depends on the number of unpaired electrons, so follow the 3d subshell across
the first transition series.
Sc(3d¹) ⇒ Ti(3d²) ⇒ V(3d³) ⇒ Cr(3d⁵) ⇒ Mn(3d⁵): electrons go into separate orbitals by
Hund's rule, so unpaired electrons keep increasing, reaching a maximum of five at manganese.
Fe(3d⁶) ⇒ Co(3d⁷) ⇒ Ni(3d⁸) ⇒ Cu(3d¹⁰) ⇒ Zn(3d¹⁰): now every further electron must pair
up with one already present, so the unpaired count falls — 4, 3, 2, 1, 0.
So the magnetic moment climbs to a peak near the middle of the series and then falls away to
zero at zinc, which is diamagnetic.
Plotted against atomic number it is an inverted V.
∴ it first increases to a maximum and then decreases.
